Fit Measures for a Structural Equation Model

Source: R/sem_fit_measures.R
sem_fit_measures.Rd

Reports in one table the measures researchers use to judge the global fit of a structural equation model: the chi square test of exact fit, the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) with its confidence interval and the tests of close and not close fit, the incremental indices CFI, TLI, NFI, IFI, and RNI, the SRMR, and gamma hat. The function takes either a fitted lavaan model, whose own statistics, sample size convention, and corrected (robust) versions it reads, or the summary statistics a paper reports, so that a published fit table can be reproduced and extended with an interval for the RMSEA and the tests it implies. A fitted model requires lavaan (in Suggests).

Usage

sem_fit_measures(
  fit = NULL,
  chisq = NULL,
  df = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  baseline_chisq = NULL,
  baseline_df = NULL,
  p = NULL,
  n_groups = 1,
  conf_level = 0.9,
  close_fit = 0.05,
  not_close_fit = 0.05,
  version = c("auto", "standard", "scaled", "robust"),
  sample_size_convention = c("N-1", "N")
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted lavaan model. It must have converged to an admissible solution, as Details describes (lavaan's post-estimation check, made on the model's own parameters when the fit has auxiliary variables). Supply either fit or the summary statistics below, not both.

chisq, df

For summary statistic input, the model's chi square test statistic \(T\) and its degrees of freedom: the likelihood ratio statistic of a normal theory maximum likelihood (ML) fit. Summary input gives the standard measures only.

N

For summary statistic input, the total sample size, summed over groups: a whole number greater than n_groups.

baseline_chisq, baseline_df

For summary statistic input, the chi square statistic and degrees of freedom of the baseline (independence) model fitted to the same data. The incremental indices need them and are NA without them. The baseline model is nested in the target model, so baseline_df must be positive and at least df.

p

For summary statistic input, the number of observed variables (not the number of parameters). Gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat need it and are NA without it; they are defined here for a single group and a covariance structure (see Details), so they are NA, with a warning, when df exceeds the \(p(p + 1)/2\) covariance moments, and df can be at most \(p(p + 3)/2\). Below that bound summary input cannot show that a model restricts the means, and supplying p states that it does not.

n_groups

For summary statistic input, the number of independent groups of a multiple group model, whose chisq, df, and N are totals over the groups. Default 1. A fitted model supplies its own number of groups.

conf_level

Confidence level of the RMSEA interval and of the gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat intervals, which come from the same noncentrality limits. Defaults to 0.90, the conventional level of the RMSEA interval, whose two limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 (see Details); conf_level = 0.95 gives 95 percent intervals.

close_fit

The RMSEA value \(\epsilon_0\) under the null hypothesis of close fit, \(H_0: \epsilon \le \epsilon_0\). Default 0.05.

not_close_fit

The RMSEA value \(\epsilon_1\) under the null hypothesis of not close fit, \(H_0: \epsilon \ge \epsilon_1\). Default 0.05.

version

Which version of the measures to report for a fitted model: "auto" (the default), "standard", "scaled", or "robust". See Details. Summary statistic input accepts "auto" and "standard", which coincide.

sample_size_convention

For summary statistic input, the multiplier \(a\) in \(T = a\hat{F}\) with which chisq was formed: "N-1" (the default), each group's sample size less one, so \(a = N - G\) for \(G\) groups, or "N", so \(a = N\). lavaan's default normal likelihood and Mplus form \(T\) with \(N\), so their statistics take "N". A fitted model supplies its own convention.

Value

A dmar_tbl (class dmar_sem_fit) with columns term and value and, always in this order, the rows chi_square, df, p_chi_square (the test of exact fit); rmsea, rmsea_ci_lower, rmsea_ci_upper; close_fit_bound, p_close_fit, not_close_fit_bound, p_not_close_fit; cfi, tli, nfi, ifi, rni; srmr; gamma_hat, gamma_hat_ci_lower, gamma_hat_ci_upper, adjusted_gamma_hat, adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_lower, adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_upper; N and n_groups. A row the input or the version does not compute is NA. The sem_fit attribute records the source, the version requested and reported and why, the statistic in the chi_square row, the correction behind the robust measures, the sample size convention and multiplier, why rows of a ULS fit of continuous data are NA (uls; NA otherwise), the boundary conventions that applied, and the lines of the printed footer.

Details

Exact Fit and the RMSEA

Write \(T\) for the model's chi square statistic on \(df\) degrees of freedom, \(a\) for the sample size multiplier with which it was formed (\(T = a\hat{F}\), where \(\hat{F}\) is the minimized fit function), \(G\) for the number of groups, and \(\alpha\) for 1 minus conf_level. The p-value of the test of exact fit (row p_chi_square) is the upper tail of the central chi square distribution at \(T\). Under a model that is wrong by an amount small relative to sampling error, \(T\) is approximately noncentral chi square with noncentrality \(\lambda = a \cdot df \cdot \epsilon^2 / G\), where \(\epsilon\) is the population RMSEA, the misfit per degree of freedom on the scale of the fit function (Steiger & Lind, 1980; Browne & Cudeck, 1993). The point estimate is \(\hat{\epsilon} = \sqrt{G \max(T - df, 0) / (a \cdot df)}\), and the confidence interval inverts the noncentral chi square distribution at \(T\) (ci_nc_chisq does the inversion) and maps its noncentrality limits to the RMSEA metric in the same way. The factor \(G\) is Steiger's (1998, Eqs. 23 and 24) multiple group RMSEA, which divides the discrepancy by the average degrees of freedom per group; applying the single group formula to a multiple group statistic gives a value too small by a factor of \(\sqrt{G}\) (Steiger, 1998, Eq. 25).

When \(T\) falls at or below the upper \(\alpha/2\) quantile of the central chi square distribution, the lower limit is 0. When it falls at or below the lower \(\alpha/2\) quantile, no noncentrality is consistent with \(T\) at that level, and the upper limit is reported as 0, as lavaan reports it and as Yuan, Chan, Marcoulides, and Bentler (2016, Eq. 4) define the corresponding T-size RMSEA, so that the upper limit and the test of not close fit always agree. This happens with probability \(\alpha/2\) for a model that fits exactly, and more often when the normal theory statistic is deflated, for example by data with light tails.

The RMSEA is conventionally reported with a 90 percent interval, the one Steiger and Lind (1980) formed from the .05 and .95 percentile points of the noncentrality, whose details Browne and Cudeck (1993) give and which lavaan's summary prints. Its two limits are the two one-sided tests at level .05 described below: a \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\) percent interval settles both tests at level \(\alpha\), so the lower limit exceeds \(\epsilon_0\) exactly when close fit is rejected, and the upper limit falls below \(\epsilon_1\) exactly when not close fit is rejected (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136 and Table 1, with one bound playing both roles). A lower limit of zero likewise says that the test of exact fit does not reject at .05. The default conf_level = 0.90 therefore gives the conventional interval, which reproduces lavaan's printed limits, and every RMSEA interval in DMAR defaults to it. conf_level = 0.95, the level of the package's other intervals, gives a wider interval whose limits decide the two tests at .025 rather than at .05. The printed table states the level beneath it.

A statistic in the millions, as from a large model fitted to a very large sample, puts the noncentrality where R's noncentral chi square distribution function, which lavaan uses, loses its accuracy (above about \(10^5\)) and then fails (above about \(2 \times 10^6\), where it once returned an interval collapsed to a point below its estimate). The limits and the tests of close and not close fit are then computed here, from the chi_square and df rows, with the Poisson mixture described in ci_nc_chisq; for a robust version whose corrected statistic DMAR cannot rebuild (FIML, ordered data, or two-stage estimation) they are NA, with a warning, once the statistic exceeds \(10^6\).

Tests of Close and Not Close Fit

The test of close fit (Browne & Cudeck, 1993) asks whether the data can reject \(H_0: \epsilon \le \epsilon_0\); its p-value is \(P\{\chi^2_{df}(\lambda_0) \ge T\}\) with \(\lambda_0 = a \cdot df \cdot \epsilon_0^2 / G\) (row p_close_fit). Failing to reject close fit does not establish it. The test of not close fit (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996) reverses the roles: it asks whether the data can reject \(H_0: \epsilon \ge \epsilon_1\), so that a small p-value, \(P\{\chi^2_{df}(\lambda_1) \le T\}\) with \(\lambda_1 = a \cdot df \cdot \epsilon_1^2 / G\) (row p_not_close_fit), is evidence that the population RMSEA is below \(\epsilon_1\). It is the equivalence test of equivalence_rmsea, which reports it with its interval and verdict. MacCallum et al. (1996) used 0.05 for both bounds, the defaults here; lavaan's default bound for not close fit is 0.08, which not_close_fit = 0.08 reproduces. These values are conventions for framing a test, not cutoffs that certify a model.

Incremental Indices

The incremental indices compare the model with a baseline model, by default the independence model, whose statistic and degrees of freedom are \(T_b\) and \(df_b\). The comparative fit index is \(CFI = 1 - \max(T - df, 0) / \max(T - df, T_b - df_b, 0)\), equal to 1 when both are zero (Bentler, 1990). Without the truncation at zero it is the relative noncentrality index, \(RNI = 1 - (T - df)/(T_b - df_b)\) (Bentler, 1990; McDonald & Marsh, 1990), which can fall outside \([0, 1]\). The Tucker-Lewis index (Tucker & Lewis, 1973), also called the nonnormed fit index (Bentler & Bonett, 1980), is \(TLI = (T_b/df_b - T/df)/(T_b/df_b - 1)\); it rewards parsimony and can also exceed 1. The normed fit index is \(NFI = (T_b - T)/T_b\) (Bentler & Bonett, 1980), and the incremental fit index is \(IFI = (T_b - T)/(T_b - df)\) (Bollen, 1989, Eq. 3). No index is clipped to \([0, 1]\), and an index whose denominator is zero or negative is NA. Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014, Eqs. 3 to 10) give the two population values these sample indices estimate: the NFI, CFI, RNI, and IFI all converge to the population CFI, \(1 - F_H/F_B\) for the population ML discrepancies of the model and the baseline (the NFI poorly, since it does not subtract the degrees of freedom), and the TLI to the population TLI, \(1 - (F_H/F_B)(df_B/df_H)\). None of them has a confidence interval here: the usual asymptotic theory assumes small misfit, which the independence model violates.

A fitted model with no degrees of freedom reproduces the moments exactly, so its statistic is zero in every version, and so is the model term \(T - c \cdot df\) of the robust indices, whatever the scaling constant \(c\), which is 0/0 there (lavaan's robust and scaled indices of such a model come out NA or not by rounding). Its CFI is therefore 1, and its RNI, NFI, and IFI are their values at a statistic of zero, those of lavaan's standard version, in every version that has them; its TLI, like the RMSEA, divides by the degrees of freedom and is NA. A model with no degrees of freedom need not fit exactly: an inequality constraint that binds, such as an error variance held at zero by bounds = "pos.var", fixes its parameter as an equality would, though lavaan does not count it among the degrees of freedom. Such a model's statistic is not zero (32.8 for one factor of three variables correlated .8, .8, and .5, \(N\) = 200), and its CFI, RNI, NFI, and IFI are formed from it (.925, .925, .926, and .926), with the standard NFI computed as \(1 - T/T_b\) where lavaan reports 1 at zero degrees of freedom; the TLI and the RMSEA rows are NA as before, and the warning and the footer say that the model does not fit exactly.

SRMR and Gamma Hat

The standardized root mean square residual (row srmr) is the root mean square of the covariance residuals, each divided by the product of the two sample standard deviations (lavaan's srmr_bentler_nomean). It is read from a fitted model and is NA for summary input. It is the same quantity in every version, since no test statistic enters it. lavaan's own srmr also averages in the mean residuals when the model has a mean structure, which makes it smaller by about \(\sqrt{t/(t + p)}\), for \(t = p(p + 1)/2\) covariance moments of \(p\) variables, when the means are saturated, as under FIML; this table keeps the covariance definition throughout. With auxiliary variables (lavaan's aux under FIML) the SRMR is over the model's own variables, the auxiliary variables set aside as in the admissibility check below. lavaan's measures average over them as well, and an auxiliary variable, a saturated correlate, adds residuals of about zero that lower the SRMR of the same model: by about 8 percent with one auxiliary variable and 15 percent with two for a three-factor model of nine items. The test statistic, and the measures built from it, compare the model with the saturated model with the auxiliary variables in both, so they need no such change. For the unbiased estimate of the SRMR, its interval, and its tests see sem_residual_fit.

Gamma hat rescales the estimated noncentrality to a goodness of fit metric, \(\hat{\gamma} = p/[p + 2(T - df)/a]\) for \(p\) observed variables, and adjusted gamma hat penalizes it for the degrees of freedom used, \(1 - [p(p + 1)/(2 df)](1 - \hat{\gamma})\), counting the \(p(p + 1)/2\) covariance moments of one group. They estimate the population values of the goodness of fit index (GFI) and the adjusted GFI that LISREL reports, which Steiger (1989) showed to be these functions of the population noncentrality for a model invariant under a constant scaling factor (a result he restates in Steiger, 1990, p. 178). Neither is truncated, so both exceed 1 when \(T < df\). Each is a monotone function of the noncentrality, so the noncentrality limits of the RMSEA interval give their limits, \(p/(p + 2\lambda/a)\) at each limit \(\lambda\) and the adjusted index of that (Steiger & Fouladi, 1997, pp. 251–252), in the rows gamma_hat_ci_lower through adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_upper. The limits are at most 1, the upper one is 1 when the lower RMSEA limit is 0, and a point estimate above 1 lies above its interval.

This gamma hat is the index lavaan 0.7-3 reports as gfi_lrt, with the same limits; lavaan caps the point estimate at 1 and reports it only when it is requested by name. The gfi lavaan prints by default is the same function of Browne's residual based (reweighted least squares) statistic in place of \(T\), which differs from gamma hat in a finite sample (0.959 against 0.957 for the three-factor model of the examples), and lavaan's gfi_lisrel and agfi_lisrel are the sample GFI and adjusted GFI of LISREL, not estimates of their population values. lavaan also reports robust versions, and so does this table: for a robust ML fit of complete continuous data with a Satorra-Bentler, Yuan-Bentler, scaled and shifted, or mean and variance adjusted statistic (MLM, MLR, MLMV, MLMVS), the robust version estimates the noncentrality as \(s(T_s - df_s)\), for the corrected statistic \(T_s\), its scaling constant \(s\), and its degrees of freedom \(df_s\), which is \(T - c \cdot df\) in each case (see the robust version below), the estimate behind the robust RMSEA of Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, and Li (2012), and takes its limits from the robust RMSEA interval; for the first three this is lavaan's gfi_lrt.robust and its limits.

Steiger's result is for covariance structures. Neither index is computed for a fitted model that restricts the means, whose statistic and degrees of freedom include the misfit and the restrictions of the means while \(p\) and \(p(p + 1)/2\) count the covariances: a growth model, or intercepts constrained equal (by a shared label, with or without lavaan's ceq.simple = TRUE), constrained to a constant, entered in a linear constraint, tied to a loading, or held at the bound of an inequality constraint (which lavaan's degrees of freedom do not count). Whether a fit restricts its means is read from the derivatives of its model implied moments, with the constraints that bind at the estimates imposed (the equality constraints, and the inequality constraints lavaan treats as active when it computes the standard errors): the means are free when the parameter directions that leave every covariance unchanged move the means in as many independent directions as there are modeled means, so that the means add no degree of freedom (the means of exogenous variables under fixed.x = TRUE are fixed at their sample values and are not counted). A mean structure whose means are free, as lavaan's default parameterization leaves them or as one indicator's intercept fixed at zero with the latent mean free leaves them, changes neither index. Summary input carries no mean structure to read, so it shows restricted means only when df exceeds \(p(p + 1)/2\), which only restricted means can produce, and the indices are then NA; below that bound they are computed from the summary statistics on the understanding that the model is a covariance structure (the statistic of a linear growth model of four waves, 12.2 on 5 df with \(N\) = 400, gives 0.991 and 0.982, which the fitted model does not). The two indices are computed for the standard and robust versions just described of a single group, single level ML fit of continuous variables without FIML or sampling weights, and for summary input when p is given, and are NA otherwise.

Standard, Scaled, and Robust Versions

A fitted model can carry more than one test statistic, and lavaan computes the fit measures from each.

"standard"

The measures above computed from the uncorrected statistic. They are the right ones for a normal theory ML fit of complete continuous data.

"scaled"

The same formulas with a scaled (or mean and variance adjusted) statistic \(T_s\) on its degrees of freedom \(df_s\) put in place of \(T\) and \(df\): the RMSEA and its interval invert the noncentral chi square at \(T_s\) on \(df_s\), the chi_square and df rows of the same table (Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, & Li, 2012, Eqs. 11 and 13, where \(df_s = df\) for a scaled statistic; Savalei, 2018, Table 1), and the tests of close and not close fit, which those sources do not treat, follow the same substitution so that they keep their duality with the interval. This is the substitution EQS and Mplus report, and the one lavaan reported when Brosseau-Liard et al. (2012, p. 911) wrote, and the one a published table of scaled measures was computed with. It is not lavaan's default for a Satorra-Bentler or Yuan-Bentler statistic (MLM, MLR) or a mean and variance adjusted one (MLMVS): lavaan 0.7-3 refers the unscaled \(T\) to the noncentral chi square on \(c \cdot df\) degrees of freedom, the trace of \(U\Gamma\) for scaling constant \(c\), which gives the same point estimate but a different interval and different close fit p-values from those the rows beside them imply. A fit made with lavaan's rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE gives the values reported here, as lavaan's default does for a scaled and shifted statistic (MLMV, WLSMV). The scaled RMSEA and CFI do not consistently estimate the population values the standard formulas define (Brosseau-Liard et al., 2012; Brosseau-Liard & Savalei, 2014; Savalei, 2018, 2021); they are offered to reproduce a published table.

"robust"

lavaan's corrected measures, which estimate the population values of the standard measures: for a robust ML fit of complete continuous data (MLM, MLR), the nonnormality corrections of Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, and Li (2012) for the RMSEA and of Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014) for the CFI, TLI, and RNI, with the correction of Savalei (2018) for a scaled and shifted statistic (MLMV). The point estimates do not depend on which corrected statistic accompanies them: each subtracts from the ML statistic \(T\) its asymptotic expectation \(c \cdot df\), with \(c\) the trace of \(U\Gamma\) over \(df\) (Brosseau-Liard et al., 2012, Appendix; Savalei, 2018, Eq. 6). lavaan computes no robust measures beside the older mean and variance adjusted statistic (MLMVS, test = "mean.var.adjusted", the statistic Savalei, 2018, Appendix B, writes \(T_{MVold}\) and no longer recommends; her mean and variance adjusted statistic is the scaled and shifted one), whose scaling constant \(s\) and degrees of freedom \(df_s\) give \(c = s \cdot df_s / df\), so they are computed here, for the model and for its baseline, with the interval and the tests of close and not close fit from \(T/c\) on \(df\) (Brosseau-Liard et al., 2012, Eq. 10); they equal lavaan's robust measures for the same model fitted by MLM, and the footer says that DMAR computed them (for a saturated model, whose \(c\) is 0/0 and whose robust CFI and RNI are 1 at a statistic of zero, nothing is computed from \(c\), and the footer names the corrections alone, as for MLM). For ordered categorical data (WLSMV), the correction of Savalei (2021); and for a FIML fit (missing = "ml"), the FIML corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023). The last are not corrections for nonnormality: they evaluate the complete data ML fit function at the FIML estimates, with the saturated FIML estimates in place of the sample moments, and so approximate the RMSEA and CFI the model would have had with complete data, whereas the uncorrected FIML indices change with the amount of missing data. lavaan uses their version 3, which does not assume normality, when the fit has a scaled statistic (MLR), and their version 6, which does, otherwise. The corrected values rest on the corrected statistic, which under FIML differs from the chi square shown in the table. After two-stage estimation they are the corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), which correct the complete data indices of the second stage for the missing data: after robust two-stage estimation (missing = "robust.two.stage") their TS V2, the version they recommend, and after normal theory two-stage estimation ("two.stage") its normal theory analog, which takes the asymptotic covariance matrix of the stage one moments to be the inverse of their observed information where TS V2 takes the sandwich of the observed and first order information, and which they did not study (see fa_confirmatory). Under FIML and two-stage estimation alike, Zhang and Savalei define only the RMSEA and the CFI; the robust TLI and RNI, the RMSEA interval, and the tests of close and not close fit are lavaan's extension of the correction. NFI and IFI have no robust version, in lavaan or here, and are NA; gamma hat has the one described above.

The default "auto" reports the robust version for a fit that carries a corrected test statistic (MLM, MLR, WLSMV, a sampling weighted fit with lavaan's default test, and the like) or uses FIML, and the standard version otherwise. A fit to ordered data by DWLS or ULS has only the standard statistic unless a corrected test is requested (it is the default test of estimator = "DWLS" and "ULS", which "WLSMV" and "ULSMV" extend with a corrected one), and lavaan gives that statistic no reference distribution, so "auto" reports its standard measures with a warning that the statistic is not chi square distributed and that a corrected test is needed for the robust measures. The same holds for a DWLS fit of continuous data whose test was set to "standard" (lavaan's default test for continuous data adds Browne's residual based statistic, which is chi square under normality and is then the one reported; the warning says to leave out test = "standard" or to use a corrected test), for a ULS fit of continuous data whose test was set so (see ULS Fits of Continuous Data), and for a sampling weighted fit whose test was set to "standard", whose statistic is a weighted pseudo likelihood ratio statistic. Full WLS is the exception among the estimators for ordered data: its weight matrix is the inverse of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the thresholds and polychoric correlations, its statistic is asymptotically chi square (Browne, 1984; Muthén, 1984), lavaan reports its p-value, and "auto" reports its standard measures without a warning (a request for the robust version says that they are the ones to report). The reason in the footer names the estimator. The measures of a ULS fit of continuous data are reported only where they do not depend on the units of the variables (see ULS Fits of Continuous Data). Browne's residual based statistic, which lavaan computes beside the standard one, is an alternative test and not a correction, and does not count. When lavaan provides a corrected statistic but no robust measures for it (and DMAR cannot compute them), "auto" reports, with a warning, the standard version for a continuous ML fit, whose standard measures estimate the population values of the ML measures as the robust ones do and the scaled ones do not (Savalei, 2018), though their interval and tests assume normal data, and the scaled version for any other fit. The chi_square, df, and p_chi_square rows show the scaled statistic under the scaled and robust versions when the fit has one, and the standard statistic otherwise. The sem_fit attribute and the printed footer name the version reported, why, and the statistic used.

ULS Fits of Continuous Data

The corrections of Brosseau-Liard and colleagues target the population discrepancy of the ML fit function. Their use with another fit function needs separate justification (Savalei, 2018). For continuous ULS, version = "robust" is therefore refused for the entire robust family, including CFI, TLI, and RNI. Invariance to multiplying every variable by the same constant is not enough to establish the population interpretation of an incremental index. This is a conservative supported-method policy, not a claim that Savalei proved every continuous-ULS index invalid. Ordered-data corrections with their own derivation are handled separately.

With ULSM or ULSMV, version = "auto" selects eligible scaled indices. These put a corrected test statistic into the index formulas; they are descriptive approximations, do not estimate ML-population fit, and have no established license to use conventional ML cutoffs. When the fit restricts means, incompatible units in the mean and covariance portions of the ULS discrepancy can make these indices change even under a common rescaling. Those rows are withheld, with the existing mean-structure qualification.

The standard statistic \(N F_{ULS}\) is in squared-covariance units. Its RMSEA and incremental indices that subtract degrees of freedom change with those units and are NA; the standard NFI, a ratio of two such statistics, remains available when eligible. This does not apply to a separately justified residual-based statistic. A fit by estimator = "ULS" alone is tested in lavaan 0.7-3 by Browne's normal theory residual based statistic, which weights the residuals by the inverse of their normal theory covariance matrix and has no units as long as the estimates at which it is evaluated do not change with the units either. They do not when the model leaves the means free, or restricts them through parameters the covariances do not share, as the equal intercepts above do, and the standard measures formed from that statistic are then reported as they are. When the model restricts the means through parameters the covariances share, as the loadings enter the means through the latent means of a multiple group model whose loadings and intercepts are equal (the scalar rung of measurement_invariance), the ULS fit function trades the mean residuals against the covariance residuals, which are in other units, so the estimates change with the units, and so do Browne's statistic and every measure formed from it: on the scalar rung of the first example of measurement_invariance, the CFI is .8874 for the raw scores and .8861 for the scores divided by 10, and the RMSEA .0680 and .0684. The RMSEA, its interval, the tests of close and not close fit, and the CFI, TLI, RNI, NFI, and IFI are then NA, with the same warning, element, and line; the chi_square row, whose chi square reference distribution holds at any root-\(n\) consistent estimates (Browne, 1984, Proposition 4), and the SRMR, which describe the fit at hand, are reported. Whether the two parts share a parameter is read from the same derivatives as whether the means are restricted: they share one when the rank of the derivatives of every model implied moment falls short of the rank of the covariance rows plus that of the mean rows. With ordered data the robust measures of a fit with "ULSMV" are the categorical correction of Savalei (2021), formed from polychoric correlations, which have no units, and none of this applies. Maximum likelihood is scale invariant; estimator = "MLR" is the estimator for nonnormal continuous data.

Two-Stage Fits

A fit by two-stage maximum likelihood (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009) fits the model to the EM estimates of the means and covariances as if they were the moments of complete data. lavaan's standard statistic for it is that naive one, which is not chi square distributed, so its standard measures (TS V0 in the terms of Zhang & Savalei, 2023) are refused, and so are its scaled measures, which put an approximate statistic into the standard formulas; the default "auto" reports the robust version. The chi_square row is then the residual based statistic of Savalei and Bentler (2009, Eq. 8; Eq. 14 with auxiliaries) after normal theory two-stage estimation (missing = "two.stage"), computed by DMAR from lavaan's moments and the observed information of the saturated model, and lavaan's scaled statistic after robust two-stage estimation (Savalei & Falk, 2014): the statistics fa_confirmatory and measurement_invariance report for the same fits. The indices are not computed from either statistic but from the naive one and its expectation, as Zhang and Savalei (2023) define them: TS V2 after robust two-stage estimation and its normal theory analog after normal theory two-stage estimation.

A case observed on an auxiliary variable (lavaan's aux) but on none of the model's variables is read by the first stage, whose EM estimates of the means and covariances it moves, and is left out of the sample size lavaan 0.7-3 reports (lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "nobs")), which counts it as empty. The naive statistic, and with it lavaan's scaled statistic, the corrected indices, the RMSEA multiplier, and the N row, then rest on fewer cases than the moments, while the residual based statistic of a normal theory two-stage fit uses every case, so the rows of the table do not describe one set of cases (and lavaan's two-stage standard errors are too large by the square root of the ratio of the two counts). sem_fit_measures() reports the rows of a fit as lavaan computed them, and warns when a fit has such cases and counts them. fa_confirmatory(missing = "two_stage") and measurement_invariance keep such cases and compute their fits again with the sample size set to every case the first stage read, so that the fits they return, and the tables of this function for them, count every case; FIML (missing = "ml") with the same auxiliary variables keeps them as well. Setting the cases aside instead would condition the analysis on an observed variable of the model, which biases the estimates when the items went missing together at random given the auxiliary variables.

The Sample Size Convention

The multiplier \(a\) must be the one with which \(T\) was formed. A fitted model supplies it: lavaan forms \(T = N\hat{F}\) for ML under its default normal likelihood, and \(T = (N - G)\hat{F}\) under likelihood = "wishart" and for the least squares estimators, and the table follows the fit, so its values equal lavaan's (for the scaled version, those lavaan gives under rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE; see above). For summary input the default "N-1" is the convention of Browne and Cudeck (1993), MacCallum et al. (1996), Kelley and Lai (2011), and DMAR's ci_rmsea, ss_aipe_rmsea, and ss_power_sem. A statistic reported by lavaan under its default likelihood or by Mplus was formed with \(N\) and takes sample_size_convention = "N". The wrong multiplier changes the RMSEA, its limits, the close fit tests, and gamma hat by an amount of order \(1/N\).

What Is Refused

A fitted model is refused when it did not converge (an error of class dmar_not_converged) and when its solution is inadmissible (a refusal of class dmar_inadmissible): fit measures of such a solution describe estimates outside the parameter space and do not speak to the specified model. A solution is inadmissible when lavaan's post-estimation check finds a negative variance estimate (a Heywood case among them) or a covariance matrix that is not positive definite: that of the latent variables, that of the residuals of the observed variables (theta), or that of the residuals of the structural part of the model (psi). The message names the variable or the matrix, and the condition carries them (see dmar_metadata). With auxiliary variables (lavaan's aux under FIML) the check is made on the model's own parameters, with the auxiliary variables set aside: lavaan models an auxiliary variable as a saturated correlate, whose covariances with the items run through their residuals, and its own check of theta, which includes those covariances, fails once an auxiliary variable is related to a factor strongly enough, however proper the model's own solution. For one factor whose items have uncorrelated residuals, and an auxiliary variable related to the items only through the factor, that happens when the squared correlation between the auxiliary variable and the factor exceeds \((1 - H) / H\), with H the maximal reliability of the factor's items (coefficient H; see reliability_H), which is a correlation above .33 when H is .9. Auxiliary variables are recognized when they are given through lavaan's aux argument; saturated correlates written into the model by hand, as semTools::cfa.auxiliary() writes them, stay in theta and are judged with it, so refit with aux to have them set aside. The same check serves sem_residual_fit, sem_information_criteria, compare_sem, ecvi, and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap, and ci_bifactor_indices judges its fit and its replications by it. Resolve the improper solution first, by changing the model or by judging that a negative variance is within sampling error of zero and fixing it, or pass the reported statistics as summary input if you accept that responsibility. Multilevel fits are refused, since one set of indices mixes the two levels; lavaan's level specific fit measures (lavaan::fitMeasures(fit, level = ...)) are the tool for them. A fit whose cases were removed by listwise deletion is evaluated on the complete cases with a warning, since that assumes the data are missing completely at random; refit it with missing = "ml" to use every case.

For a fit by normal theory two-stage estimation (missing = "two.stage") the residual based statistic, and with it the table, is refused when the fit has sampling weights or clustered cases, conditions on an observed exogenous variable (fixed.x = TRUE, the default of lavaan::sem() for a model that regresses on one, or conditional.x = TRUE), has inequality constraints or a parameter on a bound, or has auxiliary variables that the installed lavaan does not keep where DMAR reads them. Each message says what to do instead; robust two-stage estimation, whose scaled statistic lavaan computes, is the alternative throughout. A fit that conditions on an exogenous variable is refused with an error of class dmar_two_stage_fixed_x, which carries the exogenous variables, and the advice to refit with fixed.x = FALSE, and with conditional.x = FALSE too, since lavaan does not take the first beside conditional.x = TRUE. The refit leaves the estimates as they are when the exogenous variables are complete, and otherwise also keeps the cases lavaan deletes for a missing exogenous variable when it conditions on them (robust two-stage estimation deletes them too), so that its estimates differ; to keep the fit's estimates, refit on the rows the fit used, those on which every exogenous variable is observed, which lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "case.idx") lists.

Reading the Measures

No row of the table certifies a model, and the table reports no cutoff. The conventions in use are descriptions of a population RMSEA: MacCallum et al. (1996, p. 134) credit the view that values below .05 indicate close fit to Steiger (1989) and others, describe .05 to .08 as fair and above .10 as poor after Browne and Cudeck (1993), and call .08 to .10 mediocre themselves. Chen, Curran, Bollen, Kirby, and Paxton (2008) found no empirical support for .05, or any other value, as a universal cutoff: a fixed bound rejects too many correct models in samples of 100 or fewer, too few misspecified ones in samples of 800 or more, and the test of close fit with a fixed bound performs inconsistently across sample sizes, degrees of freedom, and specifications. They recommend reading the RMSEA beside the chi square statistic and the other indices rather than as a single accept or reject decision; the interval and the two tests above are how this table states the uncertainty, and the researcher chooses the bound.

The cutoffs in common use for the other indices, near .95 for the CFI and TLI, .06 for the RMSEA, and .08 for the SRMR, applied in pairs, come from the simulations of Hu and Bentler (1999), who themselves wrote that no single cutoff works equally well across conditions and that the trade-off between the two kinds of error at samples of 250 or fewer cannot be judged from the sample. Marsh, Hau, and Wen (2004) showed that the rationale behind those simulations treated a minor misspecification as a model to be rejected, so that the rules reward rejecting models that fit acceptably and cannot hold across sample sizes; they warn against reading the rules of thumb as golden rules. What a value of an index means depends on the model: on the size of the loadings and unique variances, which lower the chi square, RMSEA, and SRMR of a misspecified model when the loadings are low (Heene, Hilbert, Draxler, Ziegler, & Buehner, 2011); on the number of observed variables, which inflates the statistic and every index formed from it (Moshagen, 2012); and on the reliability of the factors, the number of items and factors, and the degrees of freedom, which is why McNeish and Wolf (2023) derive cutoffs for the model at hand by simulation, at several sizes of misspecification, so that an index reads as an effect size rather than as a verdict. This table reports the indices and their uncertainty; the bound a model is held to is a judgment about the model, stated in advance.

With few degrees of freedom the RMSEA is unstable (Kenny, Kaniskan, & McCoach, 2015): for correctly specified models with 1 to 3 degrees of freedom and \(N\) = 400, the sample RMSEA exceeded .05 in 13 to 15 percent of samples, against none at 50 degrees of freedom, and its interval at \(N\) = 50 and 1 degree of freedom was more than sixteen times as wide as at \(N\) = 1,000 and 100 degrees of freedom. They advise against computing the RMSEA when the degrees of freedom are small and suggest diagnosing poor fit by fitting the models that free the omitted parameters instead (compare_sem compares them). The interval in this table makes the instability visible rather than hiding it.

The incremental indices measure fit against the baseline model, and their metric is the baseline's misfit: under maximum likelihood the independence baseline's statistic is \(-(N - 1)\log|R|\) for the sample correlation matrix \(R\) (van Laar & Braeken, 2022). Two correctly specified models with the same chi square and RMSEA distributions have different CFI distributions when their \(|R|\) differ, and misspecified models can rank differently on the CFI and on the chi square, so a CFI is comparable across data sets only when the baselines are; van Laar and Braeken recommend reporting \(|R|\) and the baseline statistic and reading an incremental index as the share of the baseline's misfit the model removes. A fitted model's baseline statistic and degrees of freedom are lavaan::fitMeasures(fit, c("baseline.chisq", "baseline.df")); summary input takes them as given.

The raw-data H1 screen is sufficient and nonexhaustive. In models with fixed or conditional observed predictors, it screens response variables only, since predictor moments are not free. It does not assess conditional design rank or exact response-on-predictor relations. No detected obstacle is not a proof of likelihood existence or uniqueness.

Examples

# The statistics lavaan reports for the three-factor model of nine of
# the holzinger_swineford tests (N = 301), with its baseline.
# lavaan forms the statistic with N under its default likelihood.
sem_fit_measures(chisq = 85.3055, df = 24, N = 301,
                 baseline_chisq = 918.8516, baseline_df = 36, p = 9,
                 sample_size_convention = "N")
#>  term                        value   
#>  chi_square                  85.305  
#>  df                          24      
#>  p_chi_square                < 0.0001
#>  rmsea                       0.092   
#>  rmsea_ci_lower              0.071   
#>  rmsea_ci_upper              0.114   
#>  close_fit_bound             0.050   
#>  p_close_fit                 0.0007  
#>  not_close_fit_bound         0.050   
#>  p_not_close_fit             0.9993  
#>  cfi                         0.931   
#>  tli                         0.896   
#>  nfi                         0.907   
#>  ifi                         0.931   
#>  rni                         0.931   
#>  srmr                        <NA>
